This notebook uses three distinct contracts to demonstrate how uncertainty and arbitrage are expressed through the trading volume and prices of futures markets:
The S&P 500 E-mini
(Chicago Mercantile Exchange - CME)
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) Crude Oil
(CME)
Corn
(Chicago Board of Trade - CBOT)
Unlike the S&P 500 (which is cash-settled), the oil and corn contracts call for
physical delivery

of the underlying commodity at expiration. Keep in mind that physical delivery is exceedingly rare. With the exception of Treasury futures, accidentally taking physical delivery is almost always a fireable mistake!
These three contracts represent
wildly different underlying assets
, yet they
share fundamental mechanical characteristics
. Watching where these contracts align—and where they violently diverge—against the underlying Spot price will illuminate the core machinery of futures pricing.
How to Read the Upcoming Charts:
Uncertainty Transmission (Volume):
Watch how trading volume aggressively rolls from one expiring contract to the next.
The Arb Effect (Price):
Notice how the futures prices are mathematically tethered to the Spot price as expiration approaches.
Interactive Tip:
On the price charts below, click and drag your mouse across the bottom timeline to zoom in and explore specific date ranges!
Before we begin, let's lock down a couple concepts
What is the difference between cash-settled and physically delivered futures?
Cash-settled
contracts resolve by transferring the cash difference at expiration, whereas
physically delivered
contracts that aren't closed before delivery periods require the actual transfer of the underlying asset (like delivering actual barrels of oil).
Why is taking physical delivery of a commodity usually a bad idea for traders?

Most financial traders (like hedge funds) lack the infrastructure—like oil tankers, grain silos, or warehouses—needed to accept and store physical goods, making delivery logistically impossible and incredibly expensive.
How does arbitrage work in futures markets?
The relentless pursuit of risk-free profit is what physically tethers spot and futures prices together—crushing the arbitrageur's margins in the process.

Graphing Daily Futures Volume, Closing Prices, and Spot Prices 📊

children.label: Graphing Daily Futures Volume, Closing Prices, and Spot Prices 📊

children.value: By putting Volume and Price on a shared timeline, we can instantly track how market uncertainty (spikes in volume ⚡) translates into arbitrage opportunities (diverging or converging prices ⚖️) across the entire futures curve.

Doing this for a sequence of contracts (as if we had rolled our positions 🌊) demonstrates the dynamics of volume and volatility migration, revealing how they either dampen or amplify the arbitrage between Spot and futures prices.
How the Dashboard Works ⚙️
This visualization is built using the Altair library, which locks the contract data onto the exact same calendar 📅.
The Shared Timeline:
Aligns the volume plots of each contract with their corresponding Spot/settlement prices, illustrating the “magnetic pull” of expiration 🧲.
The Split View:
Separating these into two distinct upper panes allows us to quickly compare the paths of each variable—acting as a lens for market activity (volume 📊) versus valuation (price 💰).
The Interactive Arb Detail:

The bottom half of the dashboard is a dedicated “Overview and Detail” sandbox for examining how Spot and settlement prices are related. By clicking and dragging your mouse across the small timeline at the very bottom, you can instantly zoom the larger chart above it to inspect the exact spread between the futures curve and the Spot price during specific market events 🔍.
Behind the Scenes:
The custom function
graph_uncertainty_arb
generates these synchronized graphs automatically. It simply takes the DataFrames holding the data and the name of the asset (e.g., S&P 500 📈, Crude Oil 🛢️, or Corn 🌽) to build the dashboard.
🔍 Click here to view the graph_uncertainty_arb Python code

def graph_uncertainty_arb(df_list, asset):
    """
    Generates a 2-tier dashboard:
    Top Row: Static side-by-side Volume and Closing Price charts.
    Bottom Row: Interactive Overview/Detail chart explicitly for Closing Price.
    """
    # 1. Prepare the combined dataset
    df_combined = pd.concat(df_list).reset_index(names='date')

    price_domain = [df_combined['close'].min() * 0.9, df_combined['close'].max() * 1.1]
    volume_domain = [df_combined['volume'].min() * 0.9, df_combined['volume'].max() * 1.1]

    # Shared base chart ensures both rows get the legend by default
    base_chart = alt.Chart(df_combined).mark_line().encode(
        color=alt.Color('symbol:N', legend=alt.Legend(title="Symbol"))
    )

    # --- TOP ROW: Static Side-by-Side ---
    volume_chart = base_chart.encode(
        x=alt.X('date:T', title='Date'),
        y=alt.Y('volume:Q', title='Volume', scale=alt.Scale(domain=volume_domain))
    ).properties(
        width=300, height=350, title=f'{asset} Trading Volume - Full Timeline'
    )

    price_chart = base_chart.encode(
        x=alt.X('date:T', title='Date'),
        y=alt.Y('close:Q', title='Price', scale=alt.Scale(domain=price_domain))
    ).properties(
        width=300, height=350, title=f'{asset} Closing Prices - Arb Effect'
    )

    top_row = volume_chart | price_chart


    # --- BOTTOM ROW: Interactive Arb Effect (Price Only) ---
    brush = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])

    price_base = base_chart.encode(
        y=alt.Y('close:Q', title='Price', scale=alt.Scale(domain=price_domain))
    )

    # Upper Detailed Price Chart (Keeps the legend from base_chart)
    price_upper = price_base.encode(
        x=alt.X('date:T', scale=alt.Scale(domain=brush), title='')
    ).properties(
        width=650, height=260, title=f'Interactive Detail: {asset} Arb Effect'
    )

    # Lower Overview Price Chart (Legend explicitly hidden)
    price_lower = price_base.encode(
        x=alt.X('date:T', title='Date (Drag to Zoom)'),
        color=alt.Color('symbol:N', legend=None) 
    ).properties(
        width=650, height=150
    ).add_params(
        brush
    )

    bottom_row = price_upper & price_lower


    # --- FINAL DASHBOARD COMBINATION ---
    # We resolve the legend independently so Altair doesn't try to force 
    # the top row and bottom row to share a single, awkwardly placed legend.
    final_dashboard = (top_row & bottom_row).resolve_legend(
        color="independent"
    )

    return final_dashboard
🔍 Altair Graphs: Modern and Interactive Visualizations

Altair is a declarative statistical visualization library for Python. Unlike traditional plotting libraries (like Matplotlib) where you have to write code to manually draw lines, axes, and legends step-by-step, Altair lets you simply declare the links between your data columns and their visual representation.
It is built on a “grammar of graphics” and relies on three core components:
Data:
A standard Pandas DataFrame.
Marks:
The visual shape you want (e.g.,
mark_line()
mark_bar()
Encodings:
How your DataFrame columns map to visual properties (e.g., mapping the “Date” column to the X-axis, “Price” to the Y-axis, and “Symbol” to Color).
If you look at the
graph_uncertainty_arb
code above, you will see exactly how we use these three ingredients to build our complex dashboard!

Meet the Assets: Cash vs. Physical Settlement 📦

children.label: Meet the Assets: Cash vs. Physical Settlement 📦

children.value: Before we pull the data, let’s briefly review the three markets we are analyzing. Although they share the same fundamental futures mechanics, their underlying realities are wildly different:
The S&P 500 E-mini (A Reminder):
As we saw in previous chapters, the E-mini is purely financial. It is
cash-settled

, meaning at expiration, accounts are simply credited or debited in cash. There are no logistics to worry about, and arbitrage is driven strictly by the mathematical “cost of carry” (interest rates and dividend yields).
WTI Crude Oil:
Unlike an equity index, crude oil takes up physical space. WTI requires
physical delivery
of 1,000 barrels of oil per contract in Cushing, Oklahoma. Because moving millions of barrels of oil takes massive logistical planning, crude features a unique expiration calendar:
contracts expire the month
prior
to their named month.
For example, a “March” WTI contract actually stops trading in late February to give operators time to schedule pipeline space for March delivery.
Corn:

Similarly, corn requires physical delivery (typically via rail or barge). But there is an important difference—unlike oil that is drilled year-round, corn is a “grown” commodity bound by strict seasonal harvest cycles. The physical reality of storing and transporting millions of bushels of grain—combined with the massive supply volatility caused by the weather—heavily influences how its futures prices behave compared to the cash market.
📈  The S&P 500 E-mini: Pure Financial Arbitrage

children.label: 📈  The S&P 500 E-mini: Pure Financial Arbitrage

children.value: Because the S&P 500 is cash-settled, there are no pipelines, silos, or cargo ships to worry about. The arbitrage relationship here is driven almost entirely by the “cost of carry”—specifically, interest rates and dividend yields.
What to look for:

Notice how incredibly tight and predictable the price convergence is between the futures and the Spot index. In the volume chart, observe the sheer efficiency of the “roll” as institutions flawlessly migrate their massive positions to the next contract just days before expiration.

To understand the relationship between the S&P 500 Spot index and its futures contracts, we have to ask a simple question: What do you get when you hold the actual stocks that you don’t get when you hold the futures contract?
The answer comes down to two financial realities:
🔻The Cost (Interest):

Buying all 500 actual stocks requires tying up a massive amount of capital. If you buy the futures contract instead, you only have to put down a small fraction of that cash (margin), leaving the rest in the bank to earn interest.
🔺 The Benefit (Dividends):
If you hold the actual stocks, you collect cash dividends all year long. A futures contract is just an electronic “piece of paper”; it does not pay dividends.

Therefore, the arbitrage relationship here is a clean mathematical formula: the futures price must account for the interest you earn on your unspent capital, minus the dividends you forfeit by not holding the actual stocks.
🛠️ Building the S&P 500 Dashboard

Let’s put this theory to the test. In the code below, we will use our MASSIVEReader to pull a full year of quarterly S&P 500 futures contracts (from September 2025 to September 2026). Then, we will use our FredReader to grab the underlying Spot index.
By feeding them all into our
graph_uncertainty_arb
function, we can visually inspect exactly how tightly the market enforces this mathematical relationship.

# ==============================================================================
# 📈 S&P 500 DATA PIPELINE: FETCHING THE CURVE
# ==============================================================================


# 1. Fetch the Futures Contracts from MASSIVE
# We pull a sequence of quarterly E-mini S&P 500 contracts (ES).
# We specify the start and end dates to cover their active trading lifespans.
df_sep_25 = massive_data.get_futures_data('ESU5', '2025-07-01', '2025-09-19')
df_dec_25 = massive_data.get_futures_data('ESZ5', '2025-07-01', '2025-12-19')
df_mar_26 = massive_data.get_futures_data('ESH6', '2025-07-01', '2026-03-20')
df_jun_26 = massive_data.get_futures_data('ESM6', '2025-07-01', '2026-06-18')
df_sep_26 = massive_data.get_futures_data('ESU6', '2025-07-01', '2026-07-30')

# 2. Fetch the Spot (Cash) Price from FRED
# This is the actual underlying S&P 500 index—the anchor for our arbitrage.
df_sp500 = fred_data.get_series(['SP500'], start_date='2025-07-01', end_date='2026-07-30')

# Standardize the column name so our graphing function knows where to find the price
df_sp500 = df_sp500.rename(columns={'SP500': 'close'})

# ==============================================================================
# 📊 FORMATTING & GRAPHING THE S&P 500 DASHBOARD
# ==============================================================================

# 3. Create Clean Legend Labels
# We assign a readable 'symbol' string to each DataFrame.
# This ensures our Altair chart displays nice, intuitive labels (like 'DEC25')
# instead of raw ticker codes or messy file names.
df_sep_25['symbol'] = 'SEP25'
df_dec_25['symbol'] = 'DEC25'
df_mar_26['symbol'] = 'MAR26'
df_jun_26['symbol'] = 'JUN26'
df_sep_26['symbol'] = 'SEP26'
df_sp500['symbol']  = 'SPOT'

# 4. Generate the Dashboard
# Pass the list of formatted DataFrames and our title to the custom graphing function.
fq.graph_uncertainty_arb(
    [df_sep_25, df_dec_25, df_mar_26, df_jun_26, df_sep_26, df_sp500],
    'S&P 500'
)
The Takeaway
Ultimately, the tightness of this pricing isn’t magic; it is driven by the cold, mechanical reality of arbitrage.

Anxious portfolio managers perpetually agonize over their long exposures—Do I tie up cash buying 500 physical stocks to collect dividends, or buy the capital-efficient futures contract and earn interest?—arbitrageurs view this as a purely two-sided equation. When those paths get even slightly out of balance, algorithms step in, simultaneously buying the underpriced option and shorting the overpriced one. It is this relentless pursuit of risk-free gains that snaps the gap shut.
🛢️ WTI Crude Oil: Storage Costs and the Physical “Dividend”

children.label: 🛢️ WTI Crude Oil: Storage Costs and the Physical “Dividend”

children.value: With the S&P 500, the trade-off was purely financial (interest vs. dividends). But crude oil is a physical reality. To understand how it prices, we have to ask the exact same question:
What does a physical barrel of oil offer that a futures contract doesn’t?
🔻 The Cost of Physical (Storage & Tied-Up Capital):

First, physical oil requires giant steel tanks, security, and insurance. Second, buying 1,000 physical barrels ties up tens of thousands of dollars in cash. A futures contract bypasses physical storage entirely and gives you full price exposure for just a small margin deposit—leaving the rest of your cash in the bank to earn interest!
🔺 The Benefit of Physical (The Physical “Dividend”):

In commodities, we call this the “convenience yield.” If a geopolitical crisis hits and global supply pipelines freeze, a futures contract for delivery six months from now is completely useless to a refinery that needs to make gasoline
today
. Holding the actual, physical barrels right now provides a massive, immediate benefit.
📝 Moving Oil vs. Moving Data:

The fact that oil contracts must expire a full month early is the ultimate proof that you are trading a physical reality, not just a financial ticker. You can beam financial data across the globe in milliseconds, but you cannot move a million barrels of oil that fast. The market literally has to halt the financial trading early just to give the physical world time to catch up and schedule the pipeline space. Our graphs adjust for this logistical lag, making the contract legends match the actual expiration dates rather than their named contract months.
🎯 What to look for:

Look directly at early Spring 2026. At that time, physical storage was relatively cheap. As the Iran conflict escalated, the “dividend” of holding immediate physical oil skyrocketed. In the bottom chart, you will see the front-month contract and spot price shoot violently upward as panicked buyers paid a massive premium for immediate supply. How do we know this was a crisis of immediacy? The weak price response of the deferred contracts. This divergence visually captures exactly what happens when the market’s desperate need for a physical “dividend” completely overwhelms the costs of storage and interest..
🛠️ Building the WTI Crude Dashboard

Now let’s see what happens when physical constraints enter the picture. In the next cell, we will pull the futures curve for WTI Crude alongside the physical Spot price in Cushing, Oklahoma. Watch how we manually map the ticker symbols to account for that “logistic lag” (the early expiration dates) before feeding the data into our graphing function to visualize that massive 2026 convenience yield.

# ==============================================================================
# 🛢️  WTI Crude Oil DATA PIPELINE: FETCHING THE CURVE
# ==============================================================================

# We pull a sequence of quarterly WTI Crude adjusting expiration (CL)
# We specify the start and end dates to cover their active trading lifespans.
df_oct_25=massive_data.get_futures_data('CLV5','2025-07-01','2025-09-22')

df_jul_26=massive_data.get_futures_data('CLN6','2025-07-01','2026-06-22')
df_oct_26=massive_data.get_futures_data('CLV6','2025-07-01','2026-09-22')
# 2. Fetch the Spot (Cash) Price from FRED
# This is the actual underlying the anchor for our arbitrage.
df_crude=(fred_data.get_series(['DCOILWTICO'],start_date='2025-07-01',end_date='2026-09-22'))
df_crude=df_crude.rename(columns={'DCOILWTICO':'close'})

# ==============================================================================
# 🛢️ FORMATTING & GRAPHING WTI Crude Oil
# ==============================================================================

# 3. Create Clean Legend Labels
# We assign a readable 'symbol' string to each DataFrame.
# This ensures our Altair chart displays nice, intuitive labels (like 'DEC25')
# instead of raw ticker codes or messy file names.
# Adjusted for expiration not contract month

df_oct_25['symbol'] = 'SEP25'
df_jan_26['symbol'] = 'DEC25'
df_apr_26['symbol'] = 'MAR26'
df_jul_26['symbol'] = 'JUN26'
df_oct_26['symbol'] = 'SEP26'
df_crude['symbol'] = 'SPOT'

The Takeaway

The extreme price divergence you see in early 2026 isn’t the market being “wrong” about the long-term value of oil. Rather, it is the market correctly pricing desperation. When global pipelines are threatened, long-term storage models break down, and futures curves violently restructure to reflect the sheer, immediate value of having physical barrels on hand today—the
convenience yield
🌽 Corn: Location Basis and the Cost of Transportation

children.label: 🌽 Corn: Location Basis and the Cost of Transportation

children.value: With crude oil, we saw how physical storage and geopolitical panics drive the wedge between Spot and futures. But agricultural commodities introduce a different physical constraint:
Geography
🔻 The Cost of Physical (Logistics & Tied-Up Capital):

A CBOT futures contract prices the delivery of corn in the Midwest. But if you are an exporter, you need that grain down at the Gulf of Mexico. The cost to load that grain onto a barge and float it down the Mississippi River creates a massive pricing friction known as Location Basis. And just like stocks or oil, buying physical grain ties up your cash. Futures give you exposure to 5,000 bushels per contract with almost no money upfront, leaving your capital free to earn interest.
🔺 The Benefit of Physical (Immediate Export Utility):

Holding physical grain already sitting at the export terminal means you can immediately load a cargo ship bound for overseas buyers, completely bypassing the logistical delays, storage squeezes, and weather risks of the river system.
📝 A Note on the Spot Data (The “Stair-Steps”):

The Spot price used here represents the world export price at the Gulf of Mexico, published only on a monthly basis—hence the blocky, stair-step appearance of the yellow line compared to the daily futures data.
🎯 What to look for:

Notice that the futures prices never fully rise to touch the Spot price. That persistent gap between the lines is the transportation basis we just discussed—visually quantifying the exact cost of moving that corn down the river to the export terminals! In the volume chart, you can also see clear, rhythmic volume rolls as traders migrate positions according to the harvest calendar.
🛠️ Building the Corn Dashboard

Finally, let’s map the cost of geography. We will pull our CBOT Corn futures and layer them over the underlying Spot price. By passing these into our visualization tool, we will be able to clearly see the persistent gap—the location basis—that represents the physical cost of floating grain down the Mississippi River.
⚖️ A Quick Note on Units:

Before we can compare these two lines, our code has to handle a classic physical market mismatch. The global cash (Spot) price of corn is quoted in dollars per metric ton, but our CBOT futures contracts are quoted in cents per bushel. Because there are exactly 39.37 bushels in a metric ton, our code applies a conversion factor behind the scenes. We convert the Spot metric ton price down to a single bushel, and then multiply by 100 to match the CBOT cents-per-bushel quote, ensuring we are strictly comparing apples to apples!

# ==============================================================================
# 🌽 Corn DATA PIPELINE: FETCHING THE CURVE
# ==============================================================================

# 1. Fetch the Futures Contracts from MASSIVE
# We pull a sequence of quarterly Corn
# We specify the start and end dates to cover their active trading lifespans.

df_sep_25=massive_data.get_futures_data('ZCU5','2025-07-01','2026-09-12')
df_dec_25=massive_data.get_futures_data('ZCZ5','2025-07-01','2026-12-12')
df_mar_26=massive_data.get_futures_data('ZCH6','2025-07-01','2026-03-13')
df_jul_26=massive_data.get_futures_data('ZCN6','2025-07-01','2026-07-14')
df_sep_26=massive_data.get_futures_data('ZCU6','2025-07-01','2026-09-14')
# 2. Fetch the Spot (Cash) Price from FRED At Gulf Of Mexico
# This is the actual underlying the anchor for our arbitrage- (tons to bushels to cents/bushel.
df_corn_monthly=fred_data.get_series(['PMAIZMTUSDM'],start_date='2025-07-01',end_date='2026-09-14')/39.37*100
df_corn_daily=df_corn_monthly.resample('D').ffill()
df_corn_daily=df_corn_daily.rename(columns={'PMAIZMTUSDM':'close'})

# ==============================================================================
#  🌽 FORMATTING & GRAPHING Corn
# ==============================================================================

# 3. Create Clean Legend Labels
# We assign a readable 'symbol' string to each DataFrame.
# This ensures our Altair chart displays nice, intuitive labels (like 'DEC25')
# instead of raw ticker codes or messy file names.
# Adjusted for expiration not contract month


df_sep_25['symbol'] = 'SEP25'
df_dec_25['symbol'] = 'DEC25'
df_mar_26['symbol'] = 'MAR26'
df_jul_26['symbol'] = 'JUL26'
df_sep_26['symbol'] = 'SEP26'
df_corn_daily['symbol'] = 'SPOT'
fq.graph_uncertainty_arb([df_sep_25, df_dec_25, df_mar_26, df_jul_26, df_sep_26, df_corn_daily],
                       'CORN-IL. Water Way')
The Takeaway

That persistent price gap is a great reminder that when you trade an agricultural commodity, you aren’t just trading the crop itself. You are indirectly trading the river barge, the weather forecast, and the local storage silo all at once. The futures market doesn’t just price the grain; it prices the entire physical journey from the Midwest dirt to the export ship.
👀 Test Your Knowledge: Analyzing the Basis

children.label: 👀 Test Your Knowledge: Analyzing the Basis

children.value:
Use the interactive graphs above to examine the difference between the futures and spot prices (the basis).
Click the questions below to reveal the answers.
📈 For the S&P contracts, is the basis increasing or decreasing with the expiration date of the contracts?
The futures prices are consistently higher than spot prices and increase with the expiration date of the contract.
🏦 What two effects cause the pattern in the S&P basis?

This pattern occurs because the interest gained by holding cash (instead of buying the spot asset) exceeds the future value of the dividends that are "missed" by holding the futures contract rather than the underlying stocks.
🛢️ For the WTI Crude contracts, is the basis increasing or decreasing with the expiration date of the contracts?
There is no consistent pattern for the basis related to the expiration dates of the futures contracts.
⚖️ If the results are different for the S&P and WTI Crude contracts, what explains the differences?

Crude oil is purchased for the production of other commodities—most obviously gasoline. The basis is a trade-off between convenience yield, storage costs, and the interest required to hold the asset. Speculators definitely bet on these variables; however, unlike the purely financial S&P 500 contract, there is no low-risk way of physically connecting the future and the present.
🌉 Looking Ahead: From Intuition to Equation

children.value: Now that you have developed a visual intuition for how volume, Spot prices, and physical constraints interact, we are ready to ask the quantitative question: How much, exactly, is that trade-off worth?
In the next notebook, we won’t be memorizing arbitrary formulas. Instead, we are going to take the physical realities we just explored and translate them directly into the formal Cost of Carry model:
F= S + \text{Storage} - \text{Convenience or Dividend Yield} + \text{Interest}
